lesson_title: A Dimmer Switch Made from a Pencil
hook_text: Two batteries, a bulb and a pencil. Slide one clip along the pencil lead and watch the light fade. Why?
clip_script: Clip a bulb and two cells to a strip of pencil lead. Clips close together: bright bulb. Slide one clip away: the bulb fades. Nothing changed but the length of pencil lead. Electric current is the flow of charge, how many charges pass a point every second, measured in amps. The pencil lead has resistance; it makes the charges' journey harder, like a narrow bumpy road slowing traffic. More length, more resistance, less current, dimmer bulb. Thicker wire, less resistance, like a wider road. Hot metal, more resistance. And resistance is not always bad: when charges push through it, they heat it up. That is exactly how your toaster, kettle and heater work. But take away nearly all the resistance, joining a battery's ends with just a wire, and the current rushes so fast the wire can catch fire. That is a short circuit.
visual_style: A whiteboard circuit with a pencil, a clip sliding along it and a bulb fading, then a zoom into a wire with electrons bumping into atoms, then a glowing toaster.
pacing: A quick visual demo, a steady explanation, then a sharp safety warning.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and explain what makes a bulb dim.
